---
title: "Fetching from the Web"
unit: 2
cluster: "Working with APIs"
---

Programs often need something that lives on another computer: a page, a file,
or an answer worked out by a service. They get it by sending an HTTP request,
from the terminal with `curl`, or from Python with the `requests` module.

In this lesson, we'll learn how to:

* fetch a URL with `curl`, and see the request and the response
* fetch a URL from Python with `requests.get(url)`
* read the text and the status code of a response
* tell an API from a web page by its content type

## Requests and responses

A URL names something on another computer, which is called the **server**.
When you type a URL into a browser:

1. The browser connects to the server named in the URL, such as
   `figlet.apps.pipal.in`.
2. It sends a **request** to the server, asking for the rest of the URL.
3. The server sends back a **response**: a few details about the answer,
   then the answer itself.
4. The browser displays the answer.

The rules for requests and responses are called **HTTP**, which is why web
URLs start with `http://` or `https://`. The `s` in `https` stands for
secure: the connection is encrypted, so other computers on the way cannot
read it.

A browser is only one program that uses HTTP. Any program can send a request
and read the response. A URL meant for programs rather than for people is an
**API**, short for application programming interface.

Figlet is a program that draws text in large letters. The figlet API runs it
on the server. The text to draw goes at the end of the URL, after `?text=`:

```text
https://figlet.apps.pipal.in/api/figlet?text=hello
```

Open this URL in a browser, and it shows the word in large letters.

## Fetching a URL with curl

The `curl` command sends a request for a URL and prints the response. Like
any other command, it runs in a notebook with `!` in front of it. The URL is
in quotes, because `?` is a wildcard in the shell:

```python
!curl 'https://figlet.apps.pipal.in/api/figlet?text=hello'
```

The notebook displays:

```text
 _          _ _       
| |__   ___| | | ___  
| '_ \ / _ \ | |/ _ \ 
| | | |  __/ | | (_) |
|_| |_|\___|_|_|\___/ 
                      
```

The figlet program ran on the server, and only its output came back. Your
computer does not need figlet installed.

## Seeing the request and the response

The `-v` option, for *verbose*, makes `curl` print the request it sent and
the whole response. It begins with many lines starting with `*`, about
connecting to the server and making the connection secure. They are left out
here, and shown as `...`:

```python
!curl -v 'https://figlet.apps.pipal.in/api/figlet?text=hello'
```

```text
...
> GET /api/figlet?text=hello HTTP/1.1
> Host: figlet.apps.pipal.in
> User-Agent: curl/8.17.0
> Accept: */*
> 
...
< HTTP/1.1 200 OK
< Server: nginx/1.24.0 (Ubuntu)
< Date: Tue, 27 Oct 2026 23:47:18 GMT
< Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8
< Content-Length: 138
< Connection: keep-alive
< 
 _          _ _       
| |__   ___| | | ___  
| '_ \ / _ \ | |/ _ \ 
| | | |  __/ | | (_) |
|_| |_|\___|_|_|\___/ 
                      
* Connection #0 to host figlet.apps.pipal.in:443 left intact
```

The lines starting with `>` are the request. Its first line has the
**method**, `GET`, then the part of the URL after the server name, then the
version of HTTP. `GET` asks the server to send something back. The lines
after it are **headers**, extra details about the request, each written as a
name, a colon and a value. `Host` names the server, and `User-Agent` names the
program that sent the request. An empty line ends the request.

The lines starting with `<` are the response. Its first line has the version
of HTTP, then a **status code**, `200`, and its meaning, `OK`. The headers of
the response follow. `Content-Type` says what kind of text the response
carries, and `text/plain` means plain text. An empty line ends the headers,
and the **body** comes after it. The body is what the plain `curl` printed.

A browser has the same conversation with the server. It does not show the
request or the headers. It displays only the body.

## The requests module

`requests` is not part of the standard library. It is a separate package,
and the course setup has already installed it. It is imported like any other
module:

```python
import requests
```

`requests.get(url)` sends a `GET` request for `url` from Python, and returns
the response:

```python
url = "https://figlet.apps.pipal.in/api/figlet?text=hello"
response = requests.get(url)
response
```

```text
<Response [200]>
```

The value is a response object. The number in the brackets is the status
code, the same `200` that `curl -v` showed.

## The text of a response

The `text` attribute of the response is the body, as a string. An
**attribute** is a name attached to a value, like a method, but it is used
without parentheses:

```python
type(response.text)
```

```text
<class 'str'>
```

The text has several lines, so print it to see them:

```python
print(response.text)
```

```text
 _          _ _       
| |__   ___| | | ___  
| '_ \ / _ \ | |/ _ \ 
| | | |  __/ | | (_) |
|_| |_|\___|_|_|\___/ 
                      
```

## Status codes

The `status_code` attribute holds the status code of the response, as an
integer:

```python
response.status_code
```

```text
200
```

The code `200` means the request succeeded. A URL with a path that the
server does not have gives a different code:

```python
response = requests.get("https://figlet.apps.pipal.in/bad-path")
response.status_code
```

```text
404
```

The code `404` means *not found*. A failed request does not raise an error in
Python. `requests.get(url)` still returns a response, and its text is the
server's error page:

```python
print(response.text)
```

```text
<!DOCTYPE HTML PUBLIC "-//W3C//DTD HTML 3.2 Final//EN">
<title>404 Not Found</title>
<h1>Not Found</h1>
<p>The requested URL was not found on the server. If you entered the URL manually please check your spelling and try again.</p>
```

::: {.callout-warning}
A program that uses `response.text` without looking at the status code may
treat an error page as the answer. Check `response.status_code` before using
the text.
:::

The first digit of the status code tells what kind of result it is:

| Code | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `2xx`, such as `200` | the request succeeded |
| `4xx`, such as `404` | the request was wrong |
| `5xx`, such as `500` | the server failed |

## A figlet function

A function can wrap the request, so the rest of the program only deals with
text. `figlet()` takes the text to draw, adds it to the end of the URL, and
returns the body of the response:

```python
def figlet(text):
    url = "https://figlet.apps.pipal.in/api/figlet?text=" + text
    response = requests.get(url)
    return response.text
```

Each call sends a new request to the server. A loop sends one request for
each number:

```python
for n in range(5):
    print(figlet(str(n)))
```

```text
  ___  
 / _ \ 
| | | |
| |_| |
 \___/ 
       

 _ 
/ |
| |
| |
|_|
   

 ____  
|___ \ 
  __) |
 / __/ 
|_____|
       

 _____ 
|___ / 
  |_ \ 
 ___) |
|____/ 
       

 _  _   
| || |  
| || |_ 
|__   _|
   |_|  
        

```

The URL is a string, so the number is converted with `str()` before it is
added to the end of the URL.

::: {.callout-warning}
Adding the text to the end of the URL with `+` breaks when the text has a
character that means something in a URL, such as `&`, `#` or `+`. For
example, `figlet("fish & chips")` draws only `fish`, because `&` separates one
part of the URL from the next. The next lesson shows how to send such text
safely.
:::

## Web pages and APIs

The figlet server also has a web page for people, at
`https://figlet.apps.pipal.in/`. It takes the same `?text=`:

```python
page = requests.get("https://figlet.apps.pipal.in/?text=hello")
page.status_code
```

```text
200
```

The page draws the same letters, but its text is HTML, with a form, links and
styles around the drawing. A browser shows it nicely; a program would have to
dig the letters out.

The `headers` attribute holds the headers of the response. Look up
`Content-Type` in it to see what kind of text each response carries:

```python
page.headers["Content-Type"]
```

```text
'text/html; charset=utf-8'
```

```python
api = requests.get("https://figlet.apps.pipal.in/api/figlet?text=hello")
api.headers["Content-Type"]
```

```text
'text/plain; charset=utf-8'
```

The page is HTML, for a browser. The API sends plain text, which a program
can use as it is.

## Practice

### Problem 1

Run `curl -v` on the URL `https://figlet.apps.pipal.in/bad-path`. Find
the status code, its meaning and the `Content-Type` of the response in the
output.

## Summary

A request asks a server for a URL, and the response has a status code,
headers and a body; `curl` prints the response, and `requests.get(url)`
returns it to a Python program.

| Form or rule | Meaning |
|--------------|---------|
| an API | a URL meant for programs, not for people |
| `!curl 'url'` | sends a request for `url` and prints the body of the response |
| `!curl -v 'url'` | also prints the request, after `>`, and the status and headers of the response, after `<` |
| `GET` | the method of a request that asks the server to send something back |
| `import requests` | makes the `requests` module available; it is installed separately from Python |
| `requests.get(url)` | sends a `GET` request for `url` and returns a response object |
| `response.text` | the body of the response, as a string |
| `response.status_code` | the status code of the response, as an integer |
| `200` | the request succeeded |
| `404` | the server has nothing at that URL |
| `4xx` and `5xx` | the request was wrong, or the server failed |
| a failed request | still returns a response; it does not raise an error |
| `response.headers["Content-Type"]` | the kind of text in the body, such as `text/plain` or `text/html` |
